item.research_question: How does increasing the configurational entropy by introducing multiple salts into a liquid electrolyte impact the thermodynamic and kinetic properties, specifically solvation structures, ion transport, and interphase stability, in lithium batteries?
item.material_system: 0.6 M High-Entropy (HE) electrolyte composed of 0.15 M LiFSI, 0.15 M LiTFSI, 0.15 M LiDFOB, and 0.15 M LiNO3 in dimethoxyethane (DME) solvent; compared against single-salt electrolytes (0.6 M LiFSI-DME, 0.6 M LiTFSI-DME, 0.6 M LiDFOB-DME) and a 0.36 M LiNO3-DME electrolyte.
item.processing_route: Electrolytes prepared by dissolving specific amounts of lithium salts (LiFSI, LiTFSI, LiDFOB, LiNO3) in DME solvent in an Ar-filled glove box (H2O < 0.1 ppm, O2 < 0.1 ppm) at room temperature; total lithium ion concentration maintained at 0.6 M for the HE electrolyte.
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical cycling in CR2032 coin cells at room temperature; Li||LiFePO4 cells (2.5–5.0 V) for oxidation stability; Li||NCM811 cells (2.8–4.3 V) for cathode compatibility; Li||Cu cells for plating/stripping efficiency; Li||Li4Ti5O12 cells for rate capability; symmetric Li||Li cells for impedance and transference number; Cryo-TEM at -170 °C; Operando 7Li NMR; Raman spectroscopy at room temperature.
key_findings: The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte exhibits a 7Li NMR chemical shift of -0.68 ppm, indicating weaker solvation interaction compared to single-salt electrolytes (e.g., -1.19 ppm for LiTFSI-DME).
The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte shows an oxidation stability limit up to ~4.51 V, higher than the 4.36 V limit of the 0.6 M LiFSI-DME control.
Lithium plating/stripping in the 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte achieves a Coulombic efficiency of up to 98.6%, considerably higher than the 0.6 M LiFSI-DME electrolyte.
The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte has a lithium-ion transference number of 0.46 and ionic conductivity of ~12.1 mS cm−1, compared to 0.39 and 9.6 mS cm−1 for the LiFSI-DME electrolyte.
At a rate of 5.0 C, the 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte retains ~115 mAh g−1 capacity in Li||Li4Ti5O12 cells, whereas the LiFSI-DME electrolyte retains only ~40 mAh g−1.
Li||NCM811 cells with 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte achieve over 82% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 0.333 C charged to 4.3 V.
Long-term cycling at 6.0 C in Li||NCM811 cells shows ~85% capacity retention after 500 cycles and ~80% after 600 cycles.
Cryo-TEM reveals a thin (~6 nm) inorganic-rich SEI in the HE-DME electrolyte, contrasting with a thicker, non-uniform, solvent-decomposition-dominated SEI in the LiFSI-DME electrolyte.
item.mechanism: The introduction of multiple salts creates a diversity of anionic groups that participate in solvation structures, resulting in a larger variety of lithium-ion solvation environments (over 30 types predicted by DFT). This entropy-dominated diversity weakens the solvation strength between lithium ions and solvents/anions, facilitating lithium-ion diffusivity and charge transfer. The weaker solvation and diverse anion participation lead to the formation of inorganic-rich, stable interphase layers (SEI/CEI) that suppress solvent decomposition and dendrite growth.
item.limitations: The text notes that the DME solvent has relatively low oxidation stability, which is a challenge for high-voltage cathodes, although the HE electrolyte mitigates this. The study focuses on a specific four-salt prototype, and the compositional landscape is described as huge and largely unexplored.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the compositional landscape of HE materials is huge and suggest that raising entropy by introducing multiple salts can be used to improve functional properties, where the choice of specific salts and solvents should be guided by their interactions with specific anode and cathode chemistry. They also mention preparing a five-component salt HE electrolyte to support even longer stable cycling.
quotes: Unlike all liquid electrolytes so far reported, the participation of several anionic groups in this electrolyte induces a larger diversity in solvation structures, unexpectedly decreasing solvation strengths between lithium ions and solvents/anions.

The various principal anion species in the 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte result in a rich diversity of more than 30 types of lithium-ion solvation environments, much more than what is predicted for the 0.6 M LiFSI-DME electrolyte.

item.research_question: How do single and high-entropy (HE) electrolyte systems with different lithium salts and concentrations behave at the molecular level?
item.material_system: High entropy liquid electrolytes with different lithium salts in dimethoxyethane (DME) solvent; specific ratio of 1:10 salt/solvent
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with OPLS-AA force field; system packing via Packmol (60 × 60 × 60 Å box, 1200 DME + 120 salt molecules); energy minimization via conjugate-gradient; isothermal-isobaric ensemble at 300 K for 5 ns; canonical ensemble equilibration for 6 ns followed by 10 ns production run with 0.5 fs time-step; DFT calculations using Gaussian 09 with B3LYP/6-31 + G(d,p) for geometry and B3LYP/6-311 + +G(3df,3dp) for energy
item.test_conditions: 300 K (room temperature); cut-off distance of 1.1 nm for Lennard-Jones interactions; snapshots obtained every 0.5 ps
key_findings: Simulation boxes were randomly packed with 1200 molecules of DME and 120 salt molecules to achieve a 1:10 salt/solvent ratio
Isothermal-isobaric ensemble simulations at 300 K were performed for 5 ns to obtain correct volumes
Canonical ensemble simulations were continued for another 10 ns after equilibration
Radial density functions and diffusivities of lithium ions were computed using the MDAnalysis package
Solvation structures were analyzed using the Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) package
Partial charges were computed using Møller–Plesset second-order perturbation method with cc-pVTZ(-f) basis set
quotes: Molecules and ions were described by the optimized potentials for a liquid simulations all-atom (OPLS-AA) force field.
In order to create a certain concentration of salt within DME, a 1:10 salt/solvent ratio is required.
